summary: The IP subnet calculator returns ip int from the 9 fields on the form. No sign-up, no page reload, and the relationship behind it is printed below. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the IP subnet calculator work?
sections.html:
The IP subnet calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports ip int in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the network class, the subnet mask (Network details) and the subnet mask (Network details)); then you type in the figures it asks for.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

sections.title: The formula behind the IP subnet calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Ip int=(octet1, octet2, octet3, octet4)
Net address 1=(octet1, octet2, octet3, octet4, network class, subnet mask, subnet mask, subnet mask, subnet mask, 0)
Net address 2=(octet1, octet2, octet3, octet4, network class, subnet mask, subnet mask, subnet mask, subnet mask, 1)
Net address 3=(octet1, octet2, octet3, octet4, network class, subnet mask, subnet mask, subnet mask, subnet mask, 2)
Net address 4=(octet1, octet2, octet3, octet4, network class, subnet mask, subnet mask, subnet mask, subnet mask, 3)
Broad address 1=(octet1, octet2, octet3, octet4, network class, subnet mask, subnet mask, subnet mask, subnet mask, 0)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The IP subnet calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What does the IP subnet calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns ip int. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the IP subnet calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for a few values, which is 9 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (5 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the IP subnet calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. The calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
